England's Most Scenic Motorcycle Roads

England may lack Scotland's vast wilderness, but it compensates with extraordinary variety. Within a day's ride, you can traverse mountain passes, cruise coastal cliffs, weave through rolling valleys, and blast across open moorland. Here are England's finest roads for motorcyclists.

Hardknott and Wrynose Passes, Lake District

The most challenging road in England. Hardknott Pass climbs at gradients up to 33% with hairpin bends that challenge even experienced riders. Combined with the neighbouring Wrynose Pass, it's an unforgettable ride through raw Lakeland mountain scenery.

  • Distance: 10 miles (combined passes)
  • Difficulty: Hard. Steep gradients, tight hairpins, single-track.
  • Highlights: Hardknott Roman Fort at the summit, views across Eskdale, Wrynose Bottom between the passes
  • Watch out for: Oncoming traffic on blind bends, wet surface (these passes are often wet), hill starts on extreme gradients

A686 Penrith to Haydon Bridge

One of England's great cross-country roads. The A686 crosses the North Pennines through open moorland, passing Hartside Summit at 1,904ft — one of the highest A-roads in England. On a clear day, the views stretch to the Scottish borders.

  • Distance: 40 miles
  • Highlights: Hartside Summit café (a legendary biker stop), sweeping bends through moorland, the descent through the Allen Valley
  • Best for: Sweeping fast riding on open roads

A39 Atlantic Highway, North Devon/Cornwall

The A39 from Barnstaple to Bude follows the dramatic north coast of Devon and Cornwall. The road rises and falls with the coastal cliffs, offering glimpses of the Atlantic between the bends.

  • Distance: 35 miles
  • Highlights: Views across Bideford Bay, the Valley of Rocks near Lynton, coastal villages

B3306 St Ives to Land's End

Cornwall's finest coastal road. The B3306 hugs the north Cornish coast, winding through old mining villages and past abandoned engine houses with the Atlantic crashing below. The sense of being at the edge of the world is palpable.

Cat and Fiddle Road (A537), Peak District

The A537 from Macclesfield to Buxton, known as the Cat and Fiddle road, was once named Britain's most dangerous road. Today, with improved surfacing and speed restrictions, it remains one of the most enjoyable biking roads in northern England — sweeping curves through exposed moorland with vast views.

Snake Pass (A57), Peak District

The A57 from Glossop to Sheffield crosses the Dark Peak via Snake Pass. The road follows the River Ashop through wild moorland before climbing to Snake Summit. In clear weather, the sense of space is immense.

Honister Pass, Lake District

A dramatic road between Buttermere and Borrowdale, climbing past the Honister Slate Mine. Steep, narrow, and spectacular, with views down into the Buttermere valley that justify every nerve-wracking hairpin.

A170 Thirsk to Scarborough, North York Moors

This A-road crosses the North York Moors via Sutton Bank — one of England's most dramatic road climbs. The escarpment view from the top is legendary, and the road onwards through the moors to the coast is flowing and scenic.

England's best motorcycle roads aren't on motorways or dual carriageways. They're the B-roads through national parks, the single-track passes, and the coastal lanes. Slow down, explore, and the rewards are immense.

The A roads Less Travelled

  • A4069 Black Mountain Pass, Brecon Beacons border: Technically in Wales but accessible from England, this sweeping moorland road is among the best in Britain.
  • A689 across Weardale: Another North Pennine gem, quiet and flowing through beautiful dale scenery.
  • A272 across the South Downs: A gentle, scenic route through Hampshire and West Sussex villages.

England might be densely populated, but step off the motorway network and you'll find roads that rival anywhere in Europe for scenery and riding pleasure. Read our Yorkshire Dales Scenic Roads for Motorcyclists guide for more.
keyTakeaways: Hardknott and Wrynose passes in the Lake District are England's toughest tarmac, with gradients up to 33% and single-track hairpins.
The A686 over Hartside and the A170 over Sutton Bank offer fast, sweeping riding with legendary summit views.
Cornwall's B3306 from St Ives to Land's End is the finest coastal road in England.
The Cat and Fiddle (A537) and Snake Pass (A57) deliver classic Peak District moorland riding.
England's best roads are B-roads and passes through national parks, not motorways, so slow down and explore.

faq.q: How hard are the Hardknott and Wrynose passes really?
faq.a: They are the most demanding public roads in England. Hardknott hits 33% with blind hairpins and is frequently damp, so hill starts and clutch control matter. Ride them on a dry day, keep momentum without rushing, and use engine braking on the descents. Wide touring bikes and heavy pillion loads make them notably harder, so choose your moment.

faq.q: Which England road is best for confident, fast riding?
faq.a: The A686 from Penrith over Hartside Summit is the pick for flowing pace, with wide sweeping bends across open North Pennine moorland at 1,904ft. The A537 Cat and Fiddle and the A170 over Sutton Bank are similarly rewarding. All three reward smooth, sighted cornering rather than outright speed, and all attract police attention at weekends.

faq.q: When should I ride the Cornish coastal roads?
faq.a: Late spring and early autumn are ideal for the B3306 and other Cornish lanes: the weather is often kind and the roads are far quieter than the summer holiday crush. These lanes are narrow with stone walls on both sides, so summer campervan traffic makes progress slow. Early mornings give you the coast almost to yourself.

faq.q: Where are the best viewpoints to stop and photograph?
faq.a: Sutton Bank at the top of the A170 gives a vast westward panorama across the Vale of York, and Hartside Summit on the A686 looks over the Eden Valley to the Lakeland fells. In Cornwall, the abandoned engine houses near Botallack on the B3306 make dramatic foregrounds. Winnats Pass in the Peak District is a viewpoint in itself.

faq.q: Are these roads suitable in wet weather?
faq.a: Most are rideable in the wet but demand more care. The Lakeland passes are often damp even when lowland roads are dry, and their steep gradients reduce grip on climbs and descents. Peak District moorland roads can carry standing water and mud. Coastal Cornish lanes get slick with salt and diesel, so soften your inputs and leave extra braking distance.
